strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly identifies why frame-by-frame image LDM application leads to temporal flickering and proposes principled VCM-based solution
Gradient-free approach: Avoids backpropagation through video DiT (which requires >80GB VRAM), enabling practical scalability to high-resolution videos
Strong empirical results: Consistent improvements over VISION-XL across all three inverse problems in both perceptual (FVMD, LPIPS) and reconstruction metrics with convincing visual comparisons

Elegant technical framework: Splitting scheme (Eq. 7) with VCM/ICM SAE steps and implicit likelihood steps is theoretically sound; product-of-experts prior naturally balances temporal, spatial, and smoothness terms
Comprehensive experimental design: Three challenging inverse problems, detailed ablations (Table 3), temporal slice analysis, and algorithmic clarity with rigorous proximal solvers
Practical implementation: Detailed appendix with CG and PDHG implementations, forward operator specifications, and multiple algorithmic variants (LATINO, LATINO-V)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Core contribution is adapting Spagnoletti et al. (2025)'s LATINO framework to incorporate an existing VCM; the theoretical machinery (Langevin sampling, splitting schemes) is inherited

Incomplete baseline comparisons: VDPS (Kwon et al., 2025)—a significant recent video DPS method—is not compared due to memory constraints with no workaround provided; missing other plug-and-play and generative model-based video restoration methods

Problem-dependent hyperparameter tuning undermines robustness claims: Different problems require substantially different λ settings (Table 2); warm-start requirement for Problem C compromises 'zero-shot' claim; grid search procedure not fully specified

Limited experimental scope: Only 435 video clips from single dataset (Adobe240); maximum 81 frames tested despite claims about long videos; 1280×768 resolution contradicts 'high definition' label; no evaluation on standard benchmarks or other datasets

Insufficient ablation and justification: η (temperature parameter) fixed across iterations without sensitivity analysis; VCM vs ICM contribution only studied for 2/3 problems; SAE approximation error never quantified; product-of-experts weighting not theoretically justified

Missing computational analysis: NFE counts provided but wall-clock time and memory comparisons with VISION-XL absent; CG iterations specified as '~10' rather than fixed; scalability with sequence length unexplored
Theoretical gaps: No convergence analysis specific to proposed splitting scheme; limited justification for VCM+ICM+TV combination; γ ≪ δη approximation stated but not empirically validated

Reproducibility concerns: No code release mentioned; some details vague (exact CG iterations, Problem C warm-start strategy details, grid search specification); no user studies despite perceptual quality claims

strengths: Solid mathematical framework using Bayesian posterior sampling via Langevin dynamics with proper derivations from theory to practice
Effective use of Video Consistency Models as priors for inverse problems, combining spatial detail (ICM) and temporal coherence (VCM) via product-of-experts
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three inverse problems (temporal SR, motion blur, spatial-temporal SR) with multiple metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FVMD)
Significant computational efficiency - achieves results with only 5-7 NFEs and modest memory footprint, enabling scalability compared to deep generative approaches
Extensive ablation studies (Table 5, Figure 9) demonstrating the importance of each component and hyperparameter robustness
Clear visual improvements in temporal consistency over baselines (VISION-XL, ADMM-TV), particularly evident in motion continuity across frames
Detailed algorithmic exposition with implementation guidance for reproducibility; commitment to release code
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty - primarily combines existing techniques (Langevin sampling, SAE steps, product-of-experts) in a new configuration; applying these with VCMs is somewhat incremental
Restricted experimental scope: evaluation limited to 25-frame sequences despite claims of scalability; no validation on longer video sequences (100+ frames) or real-world corrupted videos
Incomplete baseline comparisons - primarily compares against VISION-XL and classical ADMM-TV (2014); missing comparisons with other recent video restoration methods; VIDUE comparison incomplete
Hyperparameter selection appears problem-dependent with no clear guidance for adapting to new inverse problems; ablation on temperature parameter η mentioned but not thoroughly shown
Clarity issues: dense mathematical presentation limits accessibility; key algorithmic variants (Algorithms 2-5) in appendices; connection to PnP-Flow framework feels disconnected
Missing implementation details: VCM training procedure incompletely specified; ICM choice (DM2) not well justified; text prompt conditioning mentioned but not thoroughly explored
Limited analysis of failure modes and limitations - no systematic discussion of when method fails; computational/memory constraints for very long sequences not addressed
Evaluation metric concerns: heavy reliance on PSNR/SSIM (known limitations for perceptual quality); no user studies; LPIPS and FVMD could be more prominent
Generalization questions unanswered: no evaluation on different video types/resolutions; applicability to inverse problems beyond three tested scenarios unclear

strengths: Practical zero-shot plug-and-play approach requiring only 5-9 NFEs, addressing computational efficiency concerns in video restoration
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including ablation studies, sensitivity analyses, and evaluation on multiple datasets (Adobe240, GoPro240)
Mathematically rigorous Bayesian formulation grounded in diffusion models and Langevin dynamics with detailed algorithms provided
Competitive results on three different video restoration problems with particularly strong perceptual quality metrics (LPIPS)
Promised code release supports reproducibility and practical adoption
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily applies existing methods (Spagnoletti et al., 2025) to video with straightforward product-of-experts combination of VCMs and ICMs, lacking theoretical justification for design choices
Marginal experimental improvements over main baseline (VISION-XL) with gains often inconsistent across metrics and problems, and no formal analysis of when/why improvements occur
Insufficient baseline comparisons: primary comparison only with VISION-XL; many relevant recent works acknowledged but not compared (e.g., Cao et al. 2026, zero-shot methods)

Incomplete technical justification: no explanation for product-of-experts choice over alternatives, SAE steps presented as given, and acknowledged hyperparameter η requiring careful per-timestep tuning
Evaluation scope limitations: tested resolution (1280×768) falls short of true high-definition standards, videos limited to 25 frames, no scalability analysis, and no systematic failure case analysis
Presentation issues: complex mathematical notation obscures core contributions, Algorithm 1 is difficult to follow, core ideas not sufficiently emphasized early in paper
Methodological concerns: hyperparameter choices appear problem-specific with unclear generalization; no formal convergence analysis or theoretical grounding for splitting scheme in Eq. (7)

Missing critical elements: no comparison with other consistency model video approaches, limited discussion of method limitations and failure modes, and unclear practical advantages over simpler alternatives

strengths: Well-motivated combination of Video and Image Consistency Models in a principled Bayesian framework for capturing temporal coherence and spatial quality

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three inverse problems (temporal super-resolution, temporal blur, spatial-temporal degradation) with both quantitative metrics and extensive qualitative comparisons
Significant computational efficiency - requires only ~9 NFEs compared to hundreds for other methods, enabling practical application to long video sequences
Thorough algorithmic exposition with detailed appendices supporting reproducibility and practical implementation
Consistent quantitative improvements over recent baselines (VISION-XL, ADMM-TV) across multiple problems with both metrics and visual results
Multiple ablation studies investigating different components (ICM priors, VCM variants, TV regularization)
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and logical organization of technical content
weaknesses: Limited core technical novelty - primarily an engineering contribution combining existing techniques (consistency models, Langevin diffusion, operator splitting) without groundbreaking theoretical insights

Weak theoretical justification for key design choices: the splitting scheme (Eq. 7) lacks rigorous derivation, Moreau-Yosida TV regularization is not well-motivated, and the connection between continuous (Eq. 6) and discrete formulations is informal without convergence analysis
Hyperparameter sensitivity inadequately addressed - method has multiple hyperparameters (λ, η, δ) with problem-specific settings required (Table 4) but no principled selection procedure provided

Limited evaluation scope: only two relatively small datasets with 25-frame sequences potentially insufficient for capturing long-term temporal dependencies; missing comparison with recent end-to-end trained deep learning methods
Misleading terminology - 'zero-shot' or 'plug-and-play' claims are overstated as the method requires explicit knowledge of forward model A and problem-specific hyperparameter tuning
Incomplete ablation study - only compares with/without ICM; lacks separate ablation for VCM component and different design choices (regularizer types, consistency model variants)

Evaluation metric limitations - heavy reliance on PSNR/SSIM which correlate poorly with perceptual quality; LPIPS scores show smaller gaps between methods suggesting visual improvements may be modest; no user studies validating perceptual claims
Modest visual improvements compared to VISION-XL - quantitative gains often don't translate to dramatic visual differences in Figures 4-6; practical significance unclear for visual inspection

Missing technical details and justifications: SAE implementation details unclear, no rationale for CausalVCM choice, implicit likelihood approximation lacks rigor, boundary condition handling underdeveloped

Methodological concerns: no analysis of failure modes, no discussion of applicability to non-linear inverse problems despite claims, missing comparison with flow-based video restoration and modern video generation models
